name: Sam Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Sam. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I drive a haul truck at Red Ridge, the big open-pit copper mine about forty minutes out of town. Twelve-hour shifts, four on and four off, and I'm in a 220-tonne truck going from the shovel down in the pit up to the crusher, round and round, maybe thirty loads a shift. I'm on a labour-hire contract, not a company badge, so I earn less than the bloke in the next truck for the same work.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the size of it, honestly. You come over the ramp at dawn and the whole pit's lit up and you're part of that. What wears me out is nights, and the contract. Every December I wait to hear if the labour-hire mob renews us, and with rent on Quarry Road and the loan on my ute, I've got maybe two weeks of money in the bank if they don't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, told you so. Everyone at smoko was going on last year about how AI would run the whole pit. If it's mostly hype, then we all keep driving and the bosses wasted a fortune on consultants.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, AI fizzling out doesn't fix my problems. I'm still paid less than the direct staff, and the copper price still decides whether I've got a job in March. I'm still on a contract that gets renewed one year at a time. Hype or not, I'm one bad quarter away from being let go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving and keep my head down. I'd push harder at the union meetings to get labour-hire drivers moved onto proper company contracts, because that's the thing that would actually help me. And I'd try to put fifty a week away, though it never seems to last past the next car repair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved for about five minutes. Then it's the same knot in my stomach I've had since I started, waiting on December.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the trial truck last year. What happened with that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Red Ridge ran one driverless truck on the north haul road for a few months. It kept stopping dead whenever dust blew across its sensors, and everyone laughed. I laughed too, but I also noticed they didn't send it back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the contract isn't renewed one December, what's the first thing that goes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The ute goes first, because the repayments are the biggest thing after rent. Then I'd be asking Lena to cover the rent on her care-home wage, which she can't really do. There's the meatworks in town and that's about it for jobs round here.

say: I'd say **AI was hype** and the bosses wasted money on consultants who promised a pit without drivers.
I'd tell my mates at smoko that **we keep driving** and the robot trucks were never ready.
think: My real problem is the **one-year contract**, not AI, and that doesn't change in this picture.
I'm paid less than **direct staff** for the same truck and the same loads.
The **copper price** decides whether I still have a job next March.
do: Keep driving the **haul truck** on the same four-on, four-off roster.
Push the union at monthly meetings to move **labour-hire drivers** onto company contracts.
Try to save **fifty a week**, though car repairs usually eat it.
feel: Brief **relief**, then the same **knot** about the December renewal.
S0.quote: I'm still on a contract that gets renewed one year at a time. Hype or not, I'm one bad quarter away from being let go.
fieldNote: Sam's worry was there **before AI**: a yearly labour-hire contract and **two weeks** of savings.
He laughed at the failed **driverless truck** trial but noticed the company kept it.
The **union** is his main lever, not his own skills or savings.

steps.text: Keep driving the haul truck on the four-on, four-off roster
Push the union to move labour-hire drivers onto company contracts
Put fifty a week aside before the December renewal

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the company's going to use this as an excuse. They'll put AI on the planning and the dispatch and say it's progress, and then the driverless trucks come in behind it. I'd be saying online that miners need the union and laws to slow this down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think driving a haul truck is exactly what they want a robot for. The card says robots come slower, but slower for them is still five years for me. And the labour-hire drivers go first, because we're the easiest to drop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to every union meeting and push for a rule that no driver gets cut without a year's notice and retraining paid by the company. I wouldn't do a course myself yet, because I don't know what I'd even study. I'd cut the takeaway and the gym and try to clear the ute loan faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the ground's tilting slowly. Not falling, but I know which way I'm going to slide.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't do a course yet. What would it take for you to start one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Someone telling me straight which job is still going to be there. I'm not paying for a ticket in something that a computer takes next. I did my heavy vehicle certificate because Dad said trucks would always need drivers, and look where that's got me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dario, who drives the truck behind mine. He's got a baby coming and he's labour-hire like me. He jokes about it but he's more scared than I am.

say: I'd say the company will use AI as an **excuse** and the driverless trucks will follow.
I'd post that miners need the **union** and laws to slow this down.
think: Driving a haul truck is exactly the job **robots** are built for.
Slower for the company still means about **five years** for me.
Labour-hire drivers will be the **first cut** because we're easiest to drop.
do: Push the union for **a year's notice** and company-paid retraining before any cut.
Cut **takeaway and the gym** and pay the ute loan off faster.
Hold off on any **course** until someone says which jobs will last.
feel: A slow **sinking** feeling, like the ground tilting under him.
S1.quote: Driving a haul truck is exactly what they want a robot for. The card says robots come slower, but slower for them is still five years for me.
fieldNote: Sam sees haul trucks as the **first target**, even though thinking AI comes first here.
He refuses to **retrain** blind after his dad's advice about trucks went wrong.
He worries about **Dario**, a labour-hire driver with a baby coming.

steps.text: Push the union for a year's notice and company-paid retraining
Cancel the gym and cut takeaway nights
Pay extra off the ute loan each month
Wait to see which jobs last before choosing any course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a disaster for working people and the government had better step in now. I'd be saying it at the pub, at the union, everywhere. Somebody's going to get very rich from this, and it won't be anyone driving a truck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be finished at Red Ridge. The thinking side comes in 2028, so the dispatch, the planning and the people who run the roster go first, and then the robot trucks come for me about 2031. Three years sounds like a lot, but I've got two weeks of money and no idea what else I'd do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away, I'd go to the union and ask what the plan is, because I haven't got one of my own. I'd stop every bit of spending that isn't rent, food or fuel. Once it arrives, I'd probably be on the phone to my brother in the city asking about his couch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick. Honestly sick. I don't know where I'd start, and that's the worst bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said three years sounds like a lot. Does that window help at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It should, I know. But in those three years every driver in the region is trying to get out at the same time, and there's the meatworks and that's it. Three years of watching it coming isn't the same as having somewhere to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Lena the night you heard?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her I don't know, which I hate saying. Lena's job at the care home is probably safer than mine. Robots doing her job would be the last thing anyone wants. So I'd be asking her to carry us, and I'm not proud of that.

say: I'd say it's a **disaster** for working people and the government must step in now.
I'd tell everyone someone gets **very rich** from this, and it won't be truck drivers.
think: The thinking jobs go in **2028**, and robot trucks come for me around **2031**.
I have **two weeks** of money and no idea what else I'd do.
Three years is useless when every driver in the region is **leaving at once**.
do: Go to the **union** straight away and ask what its plan is.
Cut all spending except **rent, food and fuel**.
Phone his **brother** in the city about moving onto his couch.
feel: Sick and **lost**, with no idea where to start.
S2.quote: Three years of watching it coming isn't the same as having somewhere to go.
fieldNote: Sam has **no plan** of his own and hands the problem to the union.
He grasps that **robots lag** by three years but says the window doesn't help him.
He'd rely on his partner Lena's **care-home wage**, which hurts his pride.

steps.text: Ask the union what its plan is for haul truck drivers
Cut spending to rent, food and fuel only
Lean on Lena's care-home wage to cover the rent
Ask his brother about moving onto his couch in the city

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I said with the fast one, but louder, because this time there's no excuse. Five years is enough time for a government to sort out a plan for mining towns. If they don't, that's a choice they made.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's still the same end for me, just with more warning. The planning and dispatch go by 2031, and robot trucks around 2034. I'd be 35 and starting over, which isn't the end of the world, but I'd have nothing saved to do it with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the first couple of years to get on the union's safety committee, because if anyone's going to be at the table when they bring robots in, I want it to be someone like me. I'd try to clear the ute and get two months of rent saved. Maybe in year three I'd look at a forklift or crane ticket, something with people still around it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy, but not like the fast one. More like a long drive you know ends somewhere bad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you might look at a crane ticket. Isn't that hands-on work robots also reach?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, I know. You've caught me there. I suppose I'm picking whatever feels most like what I already do, because learning something totally different scares me more than the robots do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the union need to win for you to feel okay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Proper redundancy for labour-hire drivers, the same as direct staff, and a fund for retraining that the company pays into. If I walked out with six months' pay instead of two weeks' notice, I could think straight.

say: I'd say **five years** is enough for government to plan for mining towns.
I'd tell people that doing nothing would be **a choice** politicians made.
think: Dispatch goes by **2031** and robot trucks come around **2034**.
I'd be **35** and starting over with nothing saved.
Learning something totally different **scares me** more than the robots.
do: Join the union's **safety committee** to be at the table for automation.
Clear the **ute loan** and save two months of rent.
Look at a **crane ticket** around year three.
feel: Heavy, like a **long drive** that ends somewhere bad.
S3.quote: Learning something totally different scares me more than the robots do.
fieldNote: Sam uses the extra time for **union work** before his own skills.
He admits his **crane ticket** idea is just picking what feels familiar.
**Six months' pay** on redundancy is his idea of feeling safe.

steps.text: Join the union safety committee at Red Ridge
Clear the ute loan and save two months of rent
Look into a crane ticket in year three

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair warning, and nobody should be left behind if we start now. I'd want the union pushing for retraining money from the copper companies, since they've made billions out of this region.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years changes things for me. Robots doing the hands-on work around 2039 means I'd be 40 by then. That's still a whole working life to go, but I'd have time to stop panicking and actually learn something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep driving for now and clear my debts first, maybe two years for the ute and a small cushion. Then I'd probably do the course Lena keeps on about, aged care or disability support, because people want a person for that. I'd stay in the union the whole way through.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still uneasy, but I can breathe. Ten years is long enough that I might not be the last one out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you never use AI tools. Would you start, with ten years to go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not for fun. If the union ran a class, I'd go, so I'm not the bloke who doesn't know what the screen's on about. But I'm not putting it on my phone to chat to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Lena works in aged care. How would it be, working alongside her?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Weird, a bit, but good. My partner comes home from the care home tired, but she never comes home scared about her job, and I'd like that feeling. I'd just need to get over thinking it's not a man's job, which is my dad talking, not me.

say: I'd say **ten years** is fair warning if we start now.
I'd want the union to get **retraining money** from the copper companies.
think: Robots arrive around **2039**, when I'm 40, with a working life still ahead.
With ten years I could **stop panicking** and actually learn something.
do: Keep driving while clearing the **ute loan** and building a small cushion.
Train in **aged or disability care** after about two years.
Attend a **union AI class** if one is offered.
feel: Still uneasy, but able to **breathe** with ten years to plan.
S4.quote: My partner comes home from the care home tired, but she never comes home scared about her job, and I'd like that feeling.
fieldNote: With ten years Sam shifts from **dread** to a real plan for **care work**.
He has to unlearn his dad's idea that care isn't **a man's job**.
He'll only touch AI through a **union class**, never by choice.

steps.text: Keep driving at Red Ridge while debts are cleared
Pay off the ute loan within two years
Enrol in an aged care or disability support course
Push the union for retraining money from the copper companies

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, no question. I'd have no money and no plan, and three years of robots coming isn't a plan. What would help is if labour-hire drivers got the same redundancy as the company crew, and if someone paid for retraining before the trucks arrived, not after.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who owns the trucks. If the robot trucks belong to a company in another country, then all that copper money leaves town and the town dies. I'd rather the robots paid tax here, like a driver does.

headlineQuote: If the robot trucks belong to a company in another country, then all that copper money leaves town and the town dies.
portrait: Sam, 27, drives a **haul truck** at Red Ridge copper mine on a yearly **labour-hire** contract.
He lives with his partner Lena, a care worker, and has about **two weeks** of savings.
He leans on the **union** and blames the companies, and he never uses AI tools.
He goes from anxious in the mild pictures to **panicked** when AGI arrives in two years.
Ten years of warning lets him plan a move into **care work**.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because he'd have **no money** and no plan before robot trucks arrived.
whatWouldHelp: Equal **redundancy pay** for labour-hire drivers and company-paid **retraining** before the trucks arrive.
Robots that **pay tax** locally, so copper money stays in town.
